intro: Section 34.2 asks what mental health is, beyond the absence of illness. It begins with why average is not the same as healthy and with the traps in any definition (context, trait versus state, and values). It then works through six models. Mental health may be above normal; a matter of maturity, traced through the adult development tasks of identity, intimacy, career consolidation, generativity and integrity; a blend of positive emotions that connect people; socioemotional intelligence; subjective well-being; or resilience, shown in the healthy involuntary coping mechanisms (humor, altruism, sublimation, suppression and anticipation). The section has no tables or figures. Update boxes correct the history of autism and the date of the first brain reward studies, and add later findings on the limbic system and triune brain idea, von Economo neurons, mirror neurons and the heritability of well-being.
objectives: Explain why mental health is more than the absence of illness and name the four problems in defining it.
Compare the six models of mental health and what each counts as healthy.
Describe the adult development tasks of Model B and the chapter's examples for each.
Contrast the connecting positive emotions of Model C with the solitary ones it leaves out, and give the chapter's brain evidence with its limits.
List the five criteria of socioemotional intelligence and the three advances in studying it.
Describe subjective well-being, how it is measured and what the chapter says about heritability and environment.
Name the three classes of coping and the five healthy involuntary mechanisms, with an example of each.
